blocks.c: The doors closed on the empty lobby with its enormous ficus and its book of names, and the car went down for another eleven seconds, and my ears popped, which they have never done in that building in fourteen months.
Minus two was a corridor of offices with the lights off and every door open.
I did not get out. I pressed it again.
Minus three was a landing, and a fire door, and a woman sitting on an upturned mop bucket next to the fire door reading a paperback by the light of a head torch.

She was maybe fifty-five. Merridew Tower facilities polo shirt, the old design, navy with the yellow logo they stopped using in the nineties. Grey in her hair. Reading glasses pushed up on her head, a second pair on her nose.

"I am." She marked her place in the paperback and stood up, and her knees cracked, and it was such an ordinary sound in such an impossible place that I nearly sat down. "Right. Three rules before you say anything else, because you're about to ask me eleven questions and the first ten are the wrong ones."

"One. Don't tell me anything you haven't written down first. Two. Whatever you do, don't tell me what it took from you tonight, and don't ask what it took from me. Three." She held up the paperback, and I saw that it was not a paperback. It was a Merridew maintenance log, 1994, blue, the twin of the one in my bag.
"Three," she said. "Whatever it tells you about me, check the book."
